bull.b: Royal Caribbean has rebuilt substantial scale and profitability, with strong revenue growth and margins following the downturn. This earnings base can support fleet investment, brand development and debt reduction, while improving operating leverage as demand and capacity continue to expand.

Record pricing, healthy booking depth and stronger onboard spending indicate durable customer demand rather than reliance only on capacity growth. Loyalty expansion and digital engagement can improve repeat visitation, direct selling and ancillary revenue across the company’s vacation ecosystem.

Refinancing floating-rate borrowings into longer-dated senior notes can reduce exposure to interest-rate volatility and improve maturity planning. Although total debt remains high, this capital-structure action supports greater financial predictability and preserves operating flexibility over the medium term.

bear.b: Leverage has improved materially from its 2022 peak but remains significant relative to equity. A demand slowdown could reduce earnings and cash available for debt service, while refinancing or interest-rate pressure could constrain investment, shareholder returns and strategic flexibility.

Strong operating cash flow has not translated into positive free cash flow after investment and working-capital effects. Persistent cash conversion weakness would make it harder to reduce leverage organically and could increase reliance on borrowing while the company continues funding fleet and destination initiatives.

Cost inflation remains a structural threat to margin durability because higher cruise costs can absorb yield gains and weaken earnings conversion. Management expects full-year costs excluding fuel to be approximately flat, but sustained pressure would limit operating leverage and cash available for reinvestment.
